'''Aude G. Billard''' (born c. August 6, 1971)<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://lasa.epfl.ch/people/member.php?SCIPER=115671|title=Aude Billard {{!}} LASA|website=lasa.epfl.ch|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> is a [[Switzerland|Swiss]] physicist in the fields of machine learning and human-robot interactions.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/author/37273980800|title=Aude Billard|website=[[IEEE]]|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> As a full professor at the School of Engineering at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne]] ([[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]]), Billard's research focuses on applying machine learning to support robot learning through human guidance. Billard's work on human-robot interactions has been recognized numerous times by the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE) and she currently holds a leadership position on the executive committee of the [[IEEE Robotics and Automation Society]] (RAS) as the vice president of publication activities.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ieee-ras.org/about-ras/governance/executive-committee|title=Executive Committee – IEEE Robotics and Automation Society|website=www.ieee-ras.org|language=en-gb|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Billard was born in [[Lausanne]], [[Switzerland]], on August 6, 1971.<ref name=":2"/> She stayed in [[Switzerland]] and pursued a Bachelor of Science in physics at the [[Swiss Federal Institute of Technology|Swiss Federal Institute of Technology at Lausanne]] ([[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]]).<ref name=":2" /> After graduating in 1994, Billard stayed at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]] for one more year to complete her Master of Science in physics.<ref name=":2" /> During her time at EPFL, she specialized in [[Particle physics|Particle Physics]] and conducted research at the [[CERN|European Center for Nuclear Research]] (CERN).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Argall|first1=Brenna D.|last2=Billard|first2=Aude G.|date=2010-10-31|title=A survey of Tactile Human–Robot Interactions|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0921889010001375|journal=Robotics and Autonomous Systems|language=en|volume=58|issue=10|pages=1159–1176|doi=10.1016/j.robot.2010.07.002|s2cid=14561706 |issn=0921-8890|via=}}</ref>

After completing her degrees at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]], Billard pursued further education at the [[University of Edinburgh]] in the Department of Artificial Intelligence.<ref name=":2" /> Billard first completed another Master of Science in 1996, this time in knowledge based systems, and then continued at the University of Edinburgh completing her PhD in artificial intelligence.<ref name=":2" />

Billard completed her PhD in 1998 and then moved back to [[Switzerland]] to pursue her postdoctoral studies at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]] and The Swiss Artificial Intelligence Lab (IDSIA or Instituto Dalle Molle di Syudi sull'Intelligenza Artificiale) until 1999.<ref name=":2" />

=== Imitative learning in social robots ===
During her master's degree at the University of Edinburgh, Billard focused on learning how to build [[Knowledge-based systems|Knowledge-Based Systems]], essentially computer programs that are built on fundamental frames, concepts, and logical assertions from the real world but with the ability to perform inferences and derive new knowledge through reasoning systems.<ref name=":2" /> Billard's Master's thesis, titled "Allo Kazam, do You Follow Me? or Learning to Speak Through Imitation for Social Robots", focused on the goal of building a system that could develop communication abilities.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://www.dai.ed.ac.uk/papers/documents/mt9607.html|title=DAI Database: MSc Thesis #9607|website=www.dai.ed.ac.uk|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> She developed a system that was capable of learning simple syntactical language and she used two mobile and autonomous robots, acting as teacher and student, to implement the architecture.<ref name=":3" /> With an emphasis on simplicity and generalizability, Billard was able to ensure that neither specificities about the environment nor the particular robotic agent were necessary for success of the architecture in practice.<ref name=":3" />

During her graduate work, Billard continued to use the teacher-learner situation as an environment with which to develop robots with social communication abilities.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|last1=Billard|first1=Aude|last2=Dautenhahn|first2=Kerstin|author2-link=Kerstin Dautenhahn|date=1999-07-15|title=Grounding Communication in Situated, Social Robots|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2812702}}</ref> Billard tested her novel learning architecture and found that learning through imitation can be achieved with simple computations and a photodetection system between the teacher and the learner to impart information about movement.<ref name=":4" /> However, Billard mentioned in her thesis there are still limitations to learning capabilities when the only means of learning is by imitation.<ref name=":4" /> Billard suggested that social learning could be enhanced with more complex cognitive mechanisms that enable a robot to associate one outcome with a subsequent event instead of with simultaneous sensory.<ref name=":4" />

=== Dynamical - Recurrent - Associative - Memory - Architecture ===
In Billard's graduate thesis, she described her work implementing imitation learning in autonomous robots through applying her innovative connectionist model designed for robot learning called DRAMA (Dynamical – Recurrent – Associative – Memory – Architecture).<ref name=":5">{{Cite thesis|title=DRAMA : a connectionist model for robot learning: experiments on grounding communication through imitation in autonomous robots|publisher=University of Edinburgh|date=1999|degree=Ph.D.|first=Aude|last=Billard|hdl=1842/34752}}</ref> To develop DRAMA, Billard used an anti-objectivist framework, distinguishing between cognitive and behavioral skills.<ref name=":5" /> This framework ensures that the behavior of one robot takes into account its previous interactions, since behaviors are performed in relation to the social environment with which the robot exists. The framework also takes into account the internal state of the robot, essentially the computations representing the robots own actions.<ref name=":5" /> She uses this model in various scenarios in which a human or a robot is the instructor teaching a student robot to build symbolic representations of the world, learn a synthetic proto-language, or perform specific imitative movements.<ref name=":5" />

During her brief postdoctoral work back at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]], Billard proposes a theoretical framework with which to understand multi-robot communication systems.<ref name=":5"/> She probabilistically modelled a multi-robot system and found that her model was able to accurately predict the ability of the system to process dynamic environmental information and apply it to communication and task learning among other robots.<ref name=":5" />

== Career and research ==
In 1999, Billard was appointed research associate in the computer science department at the [[University of Southern California]].<ref name=":2"/> The following year, she was promoted to research assistant professor, a title she held until 2002.<ref name=":2"/> She was then appointed to adjunct professor at [[University of Southern California|USC]] as well as assistant professor of the School of Engineering at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]].<ref name=":2"/> While maintaining her adjunct professorship at USC, Billard was continually promoted at EPFL. In 2005, Billard was promoted to associate professor with tenure, and then in 2013 she was promoted to full professor of the School of Engineering at EPFL.<ref name=":2"/> Her research and laboratory work have focused on using machine learning to control and design robotic systems meant to interact with humans.<ref name=":1" /> Her laboratory at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]] is called the Learning Algorithms and Systems Laboratory (LASA), which started in 2006, and is widely known for training robots to perform skills with the level of dexterity of a human.<ref name=":1" /> The main facets of research her laboratory currently explores are: human-robot interaction, machine learning with applications to robotics, fast [[adaptive control]], dexterous manipulations and grasping, as well as [[computational neuroscience]] and cognitive modelling.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=http://lasa.epfl.ch/research_new/HRI/index.php|title=Human-robot interaction {{!}} LASA|website=lasa.epfl.ch|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> All of their research works towards developing robotic systems that are able to adapt to fast changes, interact with humans and other robots in a humanistic way, and learn from teachers as well as from previous experiences.<ref name=":6" />

Billard is an active member of both the local and international research communities she is a part of. Billard is the elected president of the EPFL Teaching Body Assembly, elected president of the EPFL Teachers' Council, a member of the Swiss Science and technology Council, the Swiss Academy of Engineering Sciences,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ecmlpkdd2019.org/programme/keynotes/|title=Keynote Speakers|website=ECML PKDD 2019|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> a Fellow of the computer science department at the University of Hertfordshire, a senior editor of the IEEE ''Transactions in Robotics'', a member of the advisory board of Ecole des Mines & Telecommunication in Paris, and the associate editor of the ''International Journal of Social Robotics''.<ref name=":2"/>

Her leadership within the IEEE is longstanding as she served as an elected member of the administrative committee of the IEEE Robotics and Automation Society for two terms, from 2006 to 2011, and is currently the chair of the IEEE Robotics and Automation Society Technical Committee on Humanoid Robotics.<ref name=":1" /> From 2013 to 2014 she served as the associate editor of the IEEE Transactions in Robotics and she was the industry forum chair for the IEEE Robotics and Automation Society Committee in 2015.<ref name=":1" />

=== Improvements to imitation learning in social robots ===
In 2001, Billard proposed a biologically plausible model of human imitation and discussed its applicability in robot teaching.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|last1=Billard|first1=Aude|last2=Schaal|first2=Stefan|date=2001-01-01|title=A connectionist model for on-line robot learning by imitation|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/238124360}}</ref> The model was able to learn the principal features of an arm trajectory in a throwing/catching imitation task, was able to generalize across different demonstrations, was able to learn on-line, and its movements were robust to perturbations.<ref name=":7" /> Billard continued to explore more biologically inspired connectionist architectures with which to train robots to learn complex arm movements by imitation.<ref name="sciencedirect.com">{{Cite journal|last1=Billard|first1=Aude|last2=Matarić|first2=Maja J.|date=2001-11-30|title=Learning human arm movements by imitation:: Evaluation of a biologically inspired connectionist architecture|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0921889001001555|journal=Robotics and Autonomous Systems|series=Humanoid Robots|language=en|volume=37|issue=2|pages=145–160|doi=10.1016/S0921-8890(01)00155-5|issn=0921-8890}}</ref> She based her artificial neural networks on brain regions such as the visual and motor cortices and incorporated a decision making occurs region as well. This allowed Billard's model to imitate a teacher just as well as a human subject would imitate in the same task.<ref name="sciencedirect.com"/> Billard continues to base her computational approaches on biological systems and began to explore how implementing neuromodulatory mechanisms in neural networks produce tune-able pattern generation as they would in the human brain.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Schaal|first1=Stefan|chapter=Toward a Dynamical Systems Analysis of Neuromodulation|date=2004|chapter-url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6281988|title=From animals to animats 8: Proceedings of the Eighth International Conference on the Simulation of Adaptive Behavior|pages=334–343|publisher=MITP|isbn=978-0-262-29144-6|access-date=2020-04-12|last2=Ijspeert|first2=Auke Jan|last3=Billard|first3=Aude|last4=Vijayakumar|first4=Sethu|last5=Meyer|first5=Jean-Arcady}}</ref> Further, Billard and her colleagues began to implement neurobiological concepts such as [[homeostatic plasticity]], [[Hebbian Learning|Hebbian reinforcement learning]], and hormone feedback into their neural networks to again provide adaptability and flexibility like that exists in the human brain.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Schaal|first1=Stefan|chapter=Homeostatic Plasticity in Recurrent Neural Networks|date=2004|chapter-url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6281987|title=From animals to animats 8: Proceedings of the Eighth International Conference on the Simulation of Adaptive Behavior|pages=344–353|publisher=MITP|isbn=978-0-262-29144-6|access-date=2020-04-12|last2=Ijspeert|first2=Auke Jan|last3=Billard|first3=Aude|last4=Vijayakumar|first4=Sethu|last5=Meyer|first5=Jean-Arcady}}</ref>

In 2006, Billard began adding social cues to interactions between humanoid robots to improve the ability of humanoids to switch between learning and reproduction phases in an imitation framework.<ref name="ROMAN 2006">{{Cite book|last1=Calinon|first1=Sylvain|last2=Billard|first2=Aude|title=ROMAN 2006 - the 15th IEEE International Symposium on Robot and Human Interactive Communication |chapter=Teaching a Humanoid Robot to Recognize and Reproduce Social Cues |date=September 2006|pages=346–351|doi=10.1109/ROMAN.2006.314458|isbn=1-4244-0564-5|s2cid=17163388}}</ref> She found that implementing a gesture recognition system and using motion sensors, as well as a [[Hidden Markov model|Hidden Markov Model]] to extract the essential components of the social cues, produced more life-like behaviors in a social learning task.<ref name="ROMAN 2006"/>

=== Modelling fast adaptive control and dexterity to enable skill acquisition in robots ===
Using biologically inspired robotic models, Billard has been able to improve the ability of robots to learn precise and complex motor skills.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Billard|first=Aude|date=2001-01-01|title=Learning Motor Skills by Imitation: A Biologically Inspired Robotic Model|journal=Cybernetics and Systems|volume=32|issue=1–2|pages=155–193|doi=10.1080/019697201300001849|s2cid=18198751|issn=0196-9722|url=http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/60026/files/AB_CyberneticsSystems2000.pdf}}</ref> From 2008 on, Billard highlighted the power of [[dynamical system]]s in controlling fine robot movements and generalizing those movements within different contexts.<ref name="hersch2008">{{Cite web|last1=Hersch|first1=Micha |last2=Guenter|first2=Florent|last3=Calinon|first3=Sylvain |last4=Billard|first4=Aude| date=2008|title=Dynamical system modulation for robot learning via kinesthetic demonstrations| url=https://www.idiap.ch/~scalinon/papers/Hersch-TRO2008.pdf}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web|last1=Khansari Zadeh|first1=Seyed Mohammad|last2=Billard|first2=Aude|date=2012-05-15|title=Learning to Play Mini-Golf from Human Demonstration using Autonomous Dynamical Systems|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228975860}}</ref> Billard and her team used golf putting as a task to explore the ability of the robot to learn complex motions and adapt to changes in position, speed, and target location.<ref name=":8" /> When they allowed the robot to learn from the failed attempts at putting the golf ball into the hole, just as a human would learn from failure, the robot began to perform better as it gained information regarding the precise speed patterns and orientations from both successful and failed attempts at sinking a put.<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Citation|title=Good Golf Robots Can Sink a Putt Better Than Humans| date=17 February 2016 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XnkO8JX4QTg|language=en|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> Shortly after Billard published these astonishing results of the motor learning capabilities of robots, she showed that she could also teach robots to catch objects in flight.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kim|first1=Seungsu|last2=Shukla|first2=Ashwini|last3=Billard|first3=Aude|date=October 2014|title=Catching Objects in Flight|journal=IEEE Transactions on Robotics|volume=30|issue=5|pages=1049–1065|doi=10.1109/TRO.2014.2316022|issn=1941-0468|doi-access=free|url=https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/198748/files/TRO2316022.pdf}}</ref><ref name="sti.epfl.ch">{{Cite web|url=https://sti.epfl.ch/a-video-from-lasa-seen-more-than-1-million-times/|title=A video from LASA seen more than 1 million times – STI – School of Engineering|website=sti.epfl.ch|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> The video of their robot catching objects in flight has been viewed millions of times on YouTube and their publication in IEEE was the most frequently downloaded document in the journal.<ref name="sti.epfl.ch"/>

In 2015, Billard and her colleagues used [[Electromyography|electromyographic]] EMG recordings to decode grasping intentions at early stages of grasping, as these stages are important for early estimation of final hand position and generation of smooth gestures.<ref name=":9">{{Cite book|series=HRI'15 Extended Abstracts |year=2015|language=EN|doi=10.1145/2701973.2701997|s2cid=6757105|chapter-url = http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/224561|editor1=Batzianoulis, Iason |editor2=El-Khoury, Sahar |editor3=Micera, Silvestro |editor4=Billard, Aude |chapter=EMG-Based Analysis of the Upper Limb Motion |title=Proceedings of the Tenth Annual ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction Extended Abstracts |pages=49–50 |isbn=978-1-4503-3318-4 }}</ref> With 90% accuracy, they were able to decode three typical grasps, which provides a novel and effective approach to coordinating a subjects arm movements with a robotic hand to generate a natural pattern of motion.<ref name=":9" />

In 2016, Billard and her students won multiple awards for their paper 'Coordinated multi-arm motion planning: Reaching for moving objects in the face of uncertainty'.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://rss2016.engin.umich.edu/awards.html|title=2016 Robotics: Science and Systems|website=rss2016.engin.umich.edu|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> In this work, Billard and her students proposed a virtual object based dynamical systems control law that could generate autonomous and synchronized movements for a multi-arm robotic system. They were able to validate their approach using a dual-arm robotic system and they found that it was able to adapt and coordinate the motion of each arm to catch flying objects at high speeds and with uncertainty in trajectory.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Mirrazavi|first1=Sina|last2=Figueroa|first2=Nadia|last3=Billard|first3=Aude|title=Robotics: Science and Systems XII|date=2016-06-18|chapter=Coordinated multi-arm motion planning: Reaching for moving objects in the face of uncertainty|chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/304533127|doi=10.15607/RSS.2016.XII.019|isbn=978-0-9923747-2-3 |url=http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/218480 }}</ref>

Billard and her team have also implemented hierarchical knowledge systems to allow robots to learn both high-level complex task plans as well as lower level movements after demonstrations.<ref name=":10">{{Cite book|url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/2906831.2907006|title=Learning Complex Sequential Tasks from Demonstration {{!}} The Eleventh ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human Robot Interaction|website=dl.acm.org|series=Hri '16|date=7 March 2016|pages=611–612|language=EN|doi=10.1109/HRI.2016.7451881|isbn=978-1-4673-8370-7|s2cid=14880403|access-date=2020-04-12}}</ref> Their work in 2016 showed that by combining a variant of a Hidden Markov Model with an algorithm that outputs transition probabilities, they were able to learn both low-level motor patterns during specific behaviors as well as the probability of a transition to the next behavior in the sequence.<ref name=":10" /> Billard and her colleagues further improved robotic learning of task sequences publishing their methods in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research in 2017.<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal|last1=Medina|first1=Jose R.|last2=Billard|first2=Aude|date=2017-10-18|title=Learning Stable Task Sequences from Demonstration with Linear Parameter Varying Systems and Hidden Markov Models|url=http://proceedings.mlr.press/v78/medina17a.html|journal=Conference on Robot Learning|language=en|pages=175–184}}</ref> They combined linear parameter varying systems, to enable the learning of task sequences, with hidden Markov Models, to learn complex control policies of each subgoal/subtask, and were able to validate their approach using two different human demonstrations.<ref name=":11" />

=== Dynamical systems approach to physical human-robot interactions ===
In 2018, Billard and her colleagues developed a method to teach robots to modify their tasks based on human physical interactions and interference.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Khoramshahi|first1=Mahdi|last2=Laurens|first2=Antoine|last3=Triquet|first3=Thomas|last4=Billard|first4=Aude|title=2018 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) |chapter=From Human Physical Interaction to Online Motion Adaptation Using Parameterized Dynamical Systems |date=October 2018|pages=1361–1366|doi=10.1109/IROS.2018.8594366|isbn=978-1-5386-8094-0|s2cid=53620428|chapter-url=http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/255810/files/root_revised.pdf}}</ref> By updating the parameters of their dynamical system to account for desired trajectory versus trajectory of the human interference, they were able to test their approach in real world experiments where robots successfully learned how to adjust their movements in relation to human interactions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Khoramshahi|first1=Mahdi|last2=Billard|first2=Aude|date=2019-04-01|title=A dynamical system approach to task-adaptation in physical human–robot interaction|journal=Autonomous Robots|language=en|volume=43|issue=4|pages=927–946|doi=10.1007/s10514-018-9764-z|s2cid=67439977|issn=1573-7527|url=http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/254990/files/Khoramshahi_auto2018_task_adaptation_preprint.pdf}}</ref>

== Political career ==

A member of the [[Social Democratic Party of Switzerland]], Billard was elected in 2022 to the [[Grand Council of Vaud]] as a representative for the [[Lausanne]]-Ville district.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aude Billard, membre du Grand Conseil {{!}} VD.CH |url=https://www.vd.ch/toutes-les-autorites/grand-conseil/depute-e-s/membre-du-grand-conseil/id/625276/ |access-date=2022-08-18 |website=www.vd.ch |language=fr}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Billard is the mother of three girls.<ref name=":2"/>
